title: Yogurt vs. Kefir vs. Skyr: Nutrition Compared

seo.title: Yogurt vs. Kefir vs. Skyr: Nutrition Compared
seo.meta_description: Skyr is usually much higher in protein, while plain yogurt and kefir often provide around 3–5 g per 100 g. Fat and sugar vary by product.
seo.search_intent: Compare yogurt, kefir, and skyr for protein, fat, carbs, calcium, and fermentation.

excerpt: Plain skyr usually stands out for protein, often around 10–11 g per 100 g. Plain yogurt and milk kefir are commonly closer to 3–5 g per 100 g. Fat, sugar, and calcium vary enough by brand that the Nutrition Facts panel still matters.
content_html:
All three can look like variations on a tart white dairy food, but they are made differently. If protein is the priority, skyr usually wins clearly; if fermentation diversity is the priority, kefir has the more complex culture.

Protein is where the biggest gap appears

Plain regular yogurt commonly provides roughly 3.5–5 g of protein per 100 g. Plain milk kefir is often in the 3–4 g range. Plain skyr is usually concentrated enough to reach about 10–11 g per 100 g.

That means a 150 g serving of skyr may provide around 15–17 g of protein, versus roughly 5–7 g in the same weight of ordinary plain yogurt. Brand labels should be used for exact comparisons.

Fat depends more on the milk

Skyr is often sold low-fat or nonfat, but the category itself does not guarantee that. Yogurt and kefir can also be full-fat, low-fat, or fat-free.

Fermentation is not identical

Traditional yogurt uses defined lactic-acid bacteria. Kefir relies on a broader community of bacteria and yeasts. Skyr is cultured and then strained or concentrated, which is why protein rises per unit weight.

Fermented does not automatically mean probiotic. Harvard notes that the term probiotic should be reserved for live microorganisms with demonstrated benefits in adequate amounts.

Sugar depends on the flavoring

In plain products, much of the listed sugar is naturally occurring lactose. Fruit-flavored and sweetened versions can contain substantial added sugar, so compare like with like.

The category gives you a clue; the specific label gives you the answer.

faq.question: Which has the most protein?
faq.answer: Usually skyr, around 10–11 g per 100 g, compared with roughly 3–5 g per 100 g in regular yogurt or kefir.

faq.question: Does kefir always have more probiotics?
faq.answer: No. Live microbes and evidence vary by product, culture, and processing.

faq.question: Which has the least sugar?
faq.answer: It depends on formulation. Compare plain versions and check added-sugar labeling.
